There, seeing those two gods, practising great austerity, and himself standing in austerity there, remembering Shuka,
as long as Vyasa stayed there, Shuka, knower of supreme yoga, went to Shvetadvipa, dear one, where you went before.
There he saw the glorious Lord Narayana of manifest power, God of gods, Janardana, who is sought by the Vedas,
and, praised by Shukadeva, was pleased and spoke, O Narada. The Lord said: "I am seen by you, lord of yogis, who dwell in the secret of all gods.
You are perfected by yoga, instructed by Sanatkumara, O Brahmin; being on the path always, behold the worlds at will."
Thus addressed by Vasudeva, the son of the fire-stick bowed to him and went to Vaikuntha, honoured by all worlds, O Brahmin,
attended by gods in aerial cars, surrounded by the river Viraja; all these worlds, O Narada, shine after it as it shines,
where the stairs are of coral, adorned with gold and gems; lakes covered with lotuses, filled with the sport of divine women,
resounding with flocks of divine swans, always clear with water. There, with the four-armed gatekeepers adorned with ornaments,
followers of Vishvaksena, Siddhas, Kumuda and others, he was stopped; entering within, he saw the four-armed God of gods,
peaceful, with a gracious face, clothed in yellow silk, attended by embodied conch, discus, mace and lotus,
shining with Lakshmi on his chest and the Kaustubha, adorned with waist-cord, sacred thread, bracelets and armlets,
with a shining crown and bracelets, adorned with jewelled anklets, served day and night by the hands of Siddhas.
Seeing him, he praised Madhusudana with devotion. Shuka said: "Homage to you, Vasudeva, the sole witness of all worlds,
of the nature of the seed of the world, the full, tranquil-souled; to Hari, abiding in Vasuki, dwelling in Shvetadvipa;
to Hamsa, to him of fish form, bearing the boar's body; to Narasimha, to him worshipped by Dhruva, to the lord of Sankhya and yoga;
to the four Kumaras, to Kurma, to Prithu, the Self of his own gods; to Nabheya, the world's sustainer, the creator and the ender;
to the lord of the Bhargavas (Parashurama), to Rama, to Raghava, to the Supreme, to Krishna, maker of the Veda, to the forms of Buddha and Kalki;
to the one of fourfold manifestation, to the one to be known and meditated on, to the Supreme Self; to Vishnu named Nara-Narayana, and the one entered into Shishu;
to the one whose abode is truth, to the Ordainer, to Suparna, of self-radiance; to Ribhu, to the one called Suvrata, of good abode, and the unconquered;
to the one of universal form, who is the universe, maker of creation, preservation and end; to Sacrifice and enjoyer of sacrifice, the grossest, the atom, the seeker;
to the one with eyes of Sun and Moon, to power and strength; to the worshipful, the witness, the unborn, with many heads, feet and arms;
to the lord of Shri, the abode of Shri, subject to devotees, bearer of the Sharnga bow; to the lord of the eight Prakritis, Brahman, of infinite power;
to the one known in the Brihadaranyaka, Hrishikesha, the Ordainer; to the one with eyes like a white lotus, the knower of the field, the shining;
to Govinda, maker of the world, lord of the world, the yogi; to the true, the true to his word, Vaikuntha and Achyuta;
to Adhokshaja, Dharma, Vamana, the three-fold; to the one with ghee-bright flames, Vishnu, the infinite, and Kapila;
to Viranchi, the three-peaked, of the form of Rik, Yajus and Sama; to the one-horned, to him of pure hearing, source of the scriptures;
to Vrishakapi, the prosperous, the Lord, Vishvakarman; to the one whose form is Bhur, Bhuvah, Svah, the slayer of demons, the one without qualities;
to the stainless, eternal, imperishable, unchanging one — homage to you; protect me, O Lord, lover of those who take refuge."
Thus praised, the Lord bearing conch, discus and mace said to the son of the fire-stick, greatly fond of those who bow:
The Lord said: "O son of Vyasa, fortunate one, I am pleased with you, O firm in vows. Attain learning and devotion; you are a knower, bearing my form.
The form of mine that you saw before in Shvetadvipa, O Brahmin, I, the Sustainer of the universe, stand for the purpose of incarnation.
You are perfected, O fortunate one, by reflecting on the dharmas of liberation, like wind in the best worlds, and the sun like the sun.
You are of eternally liberated nature, worshipped by gods and men. Devotion to me, the supreme refuge of all, is hard to get in the world;
having obtained it, nothing else remains to be obtained. The sages Nara and Narayana are established in austerity until the end of the kalpa.
By their order Vyasa, O Janaka, firm in vows, will compose the Bhagavata scripture; study it. Go to earth.
He is performing austerity today on the mountain Gandhamadana, his mind distressed by separation from you; please that dear one of mine."
Thus told, Shuka, O Brahmin, bowed to the four-armed one and returned as he came to his father's side.
Then seeing him near him, the mighty son of Parashara, delighted at getting his son, ceased from austerity.
Bowing to Narayana and to Nara, best of men, accompanied by the son of the fire-stick he came to his hermitage.
By Narayana's order, through your mouth, O lord of sages, he composed the divine collection filled with various tales,
equal to the Veda, the Bhagavata, increasing devotion to Hari; and he taught it to his son Shuka, who was devoted to renunciation.
Though delighting in the Self, the Lord Shuka, son of Parashara's son, studied that collection, ever dear to Vishnu's people.
Thus these dharmas of liberation have been told to you, O sinless one; for those who read or hear them they increase devotion to Hari.
This noose of maya, with which this world is covered, runs by the impure path, ending at the digits beginning with earth.
There, standing on the circle of the earth, he is immovable or moving. The immovable are mountains, trees and the like; the moving are again threefold:
born of sweat, born of eggs, and likewise born of the womb. Among the moving and unmoving there are eighty-four lakhs of wombs.
Wandering in them, the soul by the force of karma sometimes gets a human body, the best means to all aims.
Even there, in the land of Bharata and in Brahmin and other families, birth comes only through great merit and is hard to get.
Birth is the union of man and woman, through the union of semen and blood; when a single drop enters the womb, two-natured,
then with excess of blood it is a woman, with excess of semen a man. Some soul is bound by the noose of impurity, action and the like;
then he entirely enters the state of a living being in it. Then nourished there by the food and drink brought by the mother,
the body grows there in fortnights and months. Pressed by sorrow and the like, the body covered by the membrane,
thus staying in the womb, he remembers the good and evil born of his earlier life, miserable, pressed again and again.
In the course of time the child, even while pressing his mother, himself pressed, comes out of the womb-machine head downward.
He lies motionless a moment, then wishes to cry. Then gradually the infant grows day by day,
and by stages of infancy and boyhood reaches youth. Thus in order in this world the embodied have the arising of the body.
Having obtained a human birth, hard to get and useful to all worlds, who is more sinful here than he who does not save himself?
Food, sleep, fear and sexual union are said to be common to animals and all.
One who is attached to these four only is a fool, a killer of himself. The dharma of men consists in cutting the bonds.
The cutting of the bonds of the noose arises through initiation (diksha) alone; therefore, to cut the bonds, one should receive mantra-initiation.
With bonds destroyed by the power called knowledge in initiation, the pure Self, called the principle, attains the state of nirvana.
By the vision of his own power, he meditates on and sees Shiva, and worships Shiva with mantras for the good of others.
By the radiance of Shiva's sun-power, with the eye of consciousness made capable, he sees with Shiva's power and others, his activity turned toward the Self.
The mental function of the inner organ called understanding is not able to reveal Maheshvara, because of being a noose, like a chain and the like.
Initiation alone is the supreme cause in cutting the noose; therefore by the rule stated in the scripture he should take mantra-initiation.
Having been initiated by the tantra's rule, devoted to the conduct of his own class, he should perform the practice, daily and occasional.
He should not transgress, even in mind, the conduct of his own class and stage of life. The man who receives initiation while in a stage of life
should remain in that stage and uphold its dharmas. Even actions done do not become bonds.
One karma, arising from the practice of the mantra, gives fruit; if the initiate desires enjoyments of whatever worlds,
by the power of worshipping the mantra, having enjoyed them he attains liberation. The man who, having received initiation, does not perform daily and occasional rites
becomes a ghoul for some time and at the end attains liberation. Therefore the initiate should perform daily and occasional rites and the like,
and by his practice it is inferred that he has received initiation. For the man who observes daily and occasional conduct,
liberation arises at once, from absence of any deficiency in initiation. Even there, for the one devoted to the teacher, the goal is attained, not otherwise.
Through initiation, Shiva, benefactor of all, abides in the teacher's form. For one whose devotion to the teacher is feigned for visible ends,
even done it is fruitless; expiation at every step. For one devoted to the teacher in body, mind and speech,
there is no expiation needed; success at every step. For the disciple endowed with devotion to the teacher, who offers everything,
if a mantra has been wrongly applied, the teacher would be the one to do the expiation.
A mantra in whose middle is the syllable "dar" with the pair "krodha" on the head and "astra" is said to be insulted (tiraskrita).
A mantra with the two "myo", the heart, the head, "vashat", "vaushat" in the middle, if split, is to be abandoned, giving painful fruit.
One with three syllables lacking "ham" is called "asleep" (supta); and if a vidya or mantra has seventeen syllables...
One beginning with five or six "kara" is called mad with intoxication; one with an "astra" in the middle is called fainted (murchchhita).
One with an "astra" at a pause is called deprived of vigour; one with four "astras" at the beginning, middle and head
is known as bewildered (bhranta); one with eighteen syllables, or one with twenty syllables joined with "smara" (kleem),
rich in the seeds "hrillekha" and "ankusha", is called "destroyed" (pradhvasta). A seven-syllable one is a child mantra, one of eight, a youth.
One of sixteen is young; of forty, mature; of thirty, of sixty-four, even of a hundred syllables:
a mantra of four hundred syllables is called old. A nine-syllable mantra joined with Om is called "sword" (nistrimsha).
One with the heart at the end is said to be "head-mantra"; in the middle, ... one with the "shikha" and "varma" at the end, the eye and the weapon seen —
or lacking Shiva-Shakti syllables — is said to be seedless. One in which "phat" is seen at beginning, end and middle, six times,
that mantra is without success, "slow"; a mantra of the syllable-line is the "peak" (kuta); with one syllable it is without parts.
A two-syllable one lacks strength; one of four is "keshara"; one of six is without seed; or of seven and a half syllables;
of twelve and a half syllables, it is called smoked; a mantra with three and a half seeds and twenty syllables...
one of thirty or twenty-one syllables is "embraced"; a mantra with dental letters is called bewildered.
One of twenty-four or twenty-seven syllables is to be known as hungry, devoid of mantra-success.
One of eleven or twenty-five or twenty-three syllables is called proud.
One of twenty-six, thirty-six or twenty-nine syllables is said to be defective in limbs.
One of twenty-eight or thirty-one syllables is to be known as extremely cruel, condemned in all rites.
A mantra from forty up to sixty-three syllables is to be known as "ashamed", not effective in any rites.
Mantras of sixty-five syllables are to be known as peaceful-minded; from sixty-five up to ninety-nine syllables...
those mantras are to be known as displaced, O lord of sages. Mantras of thirteen syllables and of fifteen syllables
are called "vikasa" (unblossomed) by those expert in all tantras. Those mantras counted by letters as a hundred, a hundred and fifty, two hundred,
ninety-two less one, or three hundred, are called without love.
From four hundred up to a thousand syllables, O Brahmin, they are called very large, loose in practice.
Mantras beyond a thousand syllables are called "oppressed"; those beyond that are held to be of the form of hymns.
Such mantras are declared faulty. Those who chant these mantras without knowing these faults
have no success even in hundreds of crores of kalpas. I shall tell the method for mantras spoiled by cut-off faults and the like.
One who, seated in the yoni-mudra posture, attentively chants any mantra whatever gains all successes.
Placing the left heel at the anus and the right over the banner (organ): this tying of the yoni-mudra is the best posture.
There is another method too in tying the yoni-mudra; I shall tell it to you with its secret later, Narada.
One who has received the tradition in succession, devoted to daily practice, delighted by the teacher's permission, glorious and consecrated,
handsome, pleasant-faced, tranquil, of good family, accessible, self-controlled, knowing the meaning and truth of mantra and tantra, able to restrain and to favour,
free of expectation, a sage, self-restrained, speaking what is beneficial, skilful, expert in extracting the truth, humble and well dressed,
in a stage of life, devoted to meditation, cutting doubts, intelligent, joined with daily practice — such is declared a teacher (acharya).
The disciple is peaceful, modest, pure of self, endowed with all marks, with the means of calm and the rest, faithful, of steady mind,
pure in body by food, drink and so on, righteous, pure-minded, firm in vows and conduct, grateful, afraid of sin,
his mind attached to meditation on, praise of, and service of stories of the teacher. Such should be the disciple; otherwise he gives the teacher pain.
Ravi (Sun), Ganesha, Ambika (the Goddess), Hari (Vishnu) and Shiva: with Isha, Vighna, Arka, Govinda, if Ganapati is in the middle...
Shiva, Shiva's consort, Ravi, Vishnu, with the Sun in the middle; or Ganesha, Vishnu, the Goddess and Shiva, in order.
Thus one should daily worship the group of five deities with reverence. The wise man, rising in the Brahma-muhurta and having done the necessary duties,
or unhesitating in bed, should remember on his own head, in a circle of a thousand-petalled white lotus with a pericarp,
in the triangle... the teacher, with hands giving boons and protection, two-eyed, two-armed, white, anointed with white perfumes and garlands,
with his power at his left, meditating thus and worshipping with mental offerings, the wise man should chant the Paduka mantra ten times.
(The Paduka mantra, in coded seed-syllables: "Va, Maya, Shri, Bhagendu-adhya" ... etc.)
(Continuation of the coded seed-syllables of the mantra.)
(Continuation: ... "Nandanatha ... Devi Amba ... Shri Paduka pujayami" at the heart.)
This is the Shri Paduka mantra, giving all success to men. Having offered the secret thing, the wise man should bow with these verses:

Homage to the glorious teacher by whom was shown that state which pervades the moving and unmoving, in the form of an undivided circle.

naradapuran:64:57	Homage to that teacher, whose form is the chosen deity, whose nectar-like speech destroys the poison called samsara.
Having bowed thus, he should recite the hymn that quickly produces conviction: "Om, homage to you, Lord, Shiva in the form of the teacher,
who took many forms for the accomplishment of the descent of knowledge; to the ever-new, to the one in body-form, whose sole form is the highest truth;
to the sun that dispels the darkness of all ignorance, a mass of consciousness; independent, whose body is formed of mercy, whose self is Shiva;
to the protector hereafter of devotees, the one whose form is the existence of the fortunate; to the discrimination of the discriminating, the reflection of the reflective;
to the light of lights, the knowledge-form of the knowers; homage to you in front, at the sides, behind, above and below.
Always, in the form of being-consciousness, grant me your seat. By your grace, O God, I am everywhere one whose work is done.
I am freed from the great noose of maya and death; I am Shiva, I am yours." Having thus praised, he should offer everything to the teacher.
From morning to evening, from evening to the next morning, whatever I do, O Lord of the world, let that be your worship.
Then the wise man should imagine himself washed by the stream of nectar flowing from the teacher's lotus feet, made stainless.
He should contemplate the root-vidya from the muladhara to the Brahma-aperture. Below the muladhara is a round circle of wind.
By the wind arisen from the wind-seed in it, and above it a triangular circle of fire; by the fire arisen from the fire-seed placed there,
the body that stays at the muladhara, shaped like a sleeping serpent, coiled around the self-born linga,
like a lotus-fibre, bright as ten million lightnings, very fine: having meditated on the Kula-Kundalini, he should raise her by the kurcha (technique).
Through the sushumna path, piercing the six wheels in order, by the method taught by the teacher the wise man should lead her to the Brahma-aperture.
There, immersing himself in the nectar abiding there, he should contemplate the supreme stainless, consciousness-made Self pervaded by a mass of its light.
Then, bringing her again to her own place, meditating on the God in the heart, having seen him, he should pray with mental offerings with this mantra:

O God, who are of the nature of the consciousness of the three worlds, Lord of Lakshmi, Vishnu — by your command alone, rising in the morning for your pleasure, I shall carry on the journey of samsara.
In place of 'Vishnu', O Brahmin, for another deity one should adjust. Then, for all success, he should offer the ajapa (spontaneous chant).
Six hundred by day and night, twenty-one thousand: the soul always chants the Gayatri called Ajapa.
Its seer is Hamsa, its metre is the unmanifest Gayatri; its deity is the Supreme Hamsa, with seed and power at its beginning and end.
